failure_mode: Acquisition-device variability not controlled for in validation
evidence: Chierchia et al., 2025b's limitations name motion blur and inconsistent lighting as unaddressed sources of error in consumer-grade video capture, with blur-robust reconstruction left to future work.
mitigation_note: named as an open limitation; blur robustness is quantified on the synthetic tier only, and a deblurring method is named as planned future work

failure_mode: Reference-object placement has no patient-guidance mechanism
evidence: Borst et al., 2026 (WoundAmbit) notes that accurate size estimation requires the ArUco-marker reference object to be placed approximately coplanar with the wound, and that the system lacks a mechanism to guide patients in placing it correctly. Only one partial-occlusion case was tested, so the practical frequency is unquantified.

failure_mode: Near-universal reliance on a small set of ImageNet-pretrained backbones
evidence: The non-FM cohort (48 of this step's 57 papers) concentrates on a handful of standard architectures (ResNet variants, EfficientNet, DenseNet, VGG, MobileNet, ViT, Swin), frequently fused into dual-encoder designs; Park et al., 2024 and Abdullah et al., 2026 instead run in-house self-supervised pretraining. None reports a model card or comparably structured training-data provenance statement, so whether ImageNet-derived priors capture wound-specific texture, boundary irregularity, and tissue-colour variation is not tested at either paper or field level.

failure_mode: Severe class-imbalance collapse on a minority wound type
evidence: Ni et al., 2025's best model (GoogLeNet, 88.2% overall accuracy on sharp-injury forensic classification) reached only 30.0% on its smallest class (slash wounds, 124 of 1,161 collected images) on the 212-image test set from new cases (36.7% without gamma correction), despite class-weighted random oversampling during training, against 51.7% for junior and 58.3% for senior forensic pathologists.
mitigation_note: weighted random sampling was attempted and did not prevent the collapse

failure_mode: Possible train/test leakage via post-augmentation splitting
evidence: Wang et al., 2024 augmented 146 original DFU images to 3,000 before describing its train/validation/test split, with no explicit statement that splitting occurred at the original-image level first. If augmented variants of one source image landed on both sides, the reported 98.67% accuracy would be inflated by near-duplicate leakage.
mitigation_note: not identified or addressed by the source, and not raised in its stated limitations

failure_mode: Negative transfer from insufficiently learned self-supervised pretraining
evidence: Park et al., 2024's conclusion states that downstream DFU-classification performance "largely depends on how effectively the BYOL model learns features from unlabeled data," and that performance "sometimes declined" where the unlabeled data was not sufficiently learned. The decline is asserted as observed but is not shown in any reported result: BYOL beat the supervised-only baseline at every data proportion the paper reports.
mitigation_note: the mechanism is named without a tested fix

failure_mode: "Architecturally elaborate, empirically thin" reporting
evidence: Three papers with explicit efficiency framing report no systematic inference-time, FPS, or energy benchmark: Rifat et al., 2025 (a four-component hybrid, tagged Model Selection) gives a parameter count (36.33M) but no inference measurement; Barua et al., 2026 (tagged Deployment) gives an approximate per-image latency of three to five seconds with no named model; and Bansal and Vidyarthi, 2026 (tagged Deployment), which carries "lightweight" and "real-time" in its title, reports efficiency only qualitatively. The pattern recurs whether or not a paper presents itself as deployment-focused.

failure_mode: Near-saturated accuracy claims warrant independent replication
evidence: Kiprono, 2025 reported 99.90% ensemble accuracy on a single curated dataset, including 100.00% for one constituent backbone. No other paper in this corpus has replicated the result.

failure_mode: Internal validation accuracy does not predict external generalization
evidence: Asare et al., 2026's segmentation model reached Dice 0.89 on its own held-out split and 0.62 on zero-shot external transfer to AZH (0.785 on a second external set, Medetec). The source frames this positively, as evidence of robust zero-shot transferability, and makes deployment-readiness claims alongside a call for multi-centre validation.
mitigation_note: multi-centre validation named as needed, not carried out

failure_mode: MedSAM underperforms generic SAM, replicated across two wound types
evidence: Wang et al., 2026b found MedSAM inferior to vanilla SAM on pediatric burn images (Dice 0.80 vs 0.90 with box prompts; 0.72 vs 0.86 with a single box). Taipe et al., 2024 found the same direction on DFU segmentation, MedSAM the worst of five SAM variants (IoU 0.568 against 0.941 for the best engineered zero-shot prompt). The comparators differ, so the two gaps are not on a directly comparable scale; in both, broad medical-domain fine-tuning was associated with lower performance on wound images.
mitigation_note: both papers build from vanilla SAM instead of MedSAM, Taipe et al. by prompt engineering and Wang et al. by burn-specific fine-tuning; neither fixes MedSAM

failure_mode: Well-engineered prompting can beat fine-tuning outright
evidence: Taipe et al., 2024's combined zero-shot SAM prompt (YOLOv5-derived boxes plus superpixel-derived points) reached IoU 0.941 / Dice 0.969, beating a fine-tuned SAM baseline (IoU 0.873 / Dice 0.928) on the same DFU test set. The authors describe prompt engineering as "a viable alternative to SAM's fine-tuning." This is a counter-example to reading the adaptation-intensity spectrum as a maturity ladder.
mitigation_note: itself a working, lower-cost alternative, demonstrated on one dataset and etiology

failure_mode: FM-based approaches degrade less under distribution shift than purpose-built CNN baselines
evidence: Hamrani et al., 2025 and Zhao et al., 2026 each report smaller drops on external data for text-conditioned foundation-model systems (a text-guided diffusion model in Hamrani et al.; GLIP in Zhao et al.) than for conventional baselines. In Zhao et al., 2026, a Faster R-CNN detector's mAP@0.5 fell from 48.35% to 20.54% under external validation while its GLIP-based ensemble system fell from 68.50% to 57.85% (GLIP-T with its SIAF module: 61.55% to 50.01%). Hamrani et al.'s external comparison uses approximate medians read from a figure for a 40-image in-house set (about 75% Dice against about 45% for FUSegNet). The claim concerns relative performance only: Baseman et al., 2025 outperformed all five of its non-FM baselines on its naturalistic cohort and still reached only 54.4% Dice.
mitigation_note: , and only in that relative sense

failure_mode: Multimodal fusion gains are task- and configuration-dependent
evidence: Mousa et al., 2025 fused RGB wound images (ViT branch) with body-location data (transformer branch) for wound-type classification on 730 AZH images. On the 4-class body-map task the best image-only configuration reached 0.8301 accuracy (ViT with wavelet features and MGTO tuning) while image-plus-location variants reached 0.8007, 0.8123, 0.8342, and 0.8232 depending on the metaheuristic, so three of four fusion configurations fell below the best image-only result. On the 6-class task, by contrast, image-plus-location fusion was best (0.8644 against 0.8401 image-only). The benefit of location data therefore depends on the task and the optimizer.
mitigation_note: no configuration-selection method is proposed that would reliably capture the best-case result

failure_mode: Hallucination in FM-generated clinical descriptions
evidence: Busaranuvong et al., 2026a states that "the primary drawback of our framework is the occasional incorrect Wound-BLIP image descriptions, likely due to inaccuracy in the GPT-4o-generated data used for fine-tuning Wound-BLIP." Separately, Choudhary et al., 2025 documented a zero-shot medical VLM (Lingshu-7B) stating unsupported specifics, including time elapsed since surgery, which is not visible in any image, in 2 of its 7 qualitative examples; per the authors, only one of the seven mentions both the incision and infection.
mitigation_note: both name the mechanism without testing a fix

failure_mode: A specific tissue-colour hallucination example
evidence: Chang et al., 2025's qualitative example table (in the authors' English translation of Chinese output) shows a generated description reading "partially red" where the clinical reference reads "partially pink" for the same Stage 4 pressure-injury image; the generated text also drops "necrotic." The error is a clinically meaningful visual-attribute error in the paper's own reported example and is not flagged by its authors.

failure_mode: Stage 3/4 pressure-injury boundary confusion, reported in two papers
evidence: Chang et al., 2025 reports Stage 3 as its weakest F1 (73.17%, lowest of six grades), and Lott et al., 2026's per-stage deferral analysis gives Stage 3 the highest deferral rate (68.3%). Fard et al., 2025a attributes Stage III/IV difficulty to prior work and reports better III/IV consistency for its own model, although its confusion matrix still shows Stage III/IV as the largest residual off-diagonal band (21 of roughly 37 errors).
mitigation_note: Lott et al., 2026's selective-prediction mechanism lets the system abstain more often on Stage 3, managing the error without resolving the underlying confusion

failure_mode: Quantified label noise and evaluator disagreement
evidence: Fard et al., 2025a reports a wound-care clinician with over 35 years of experience disagreeing with the PIID dataset's own ground-truth pressure-injury stage in 36 of 84 reviewed images (43%). Basiri et al., 2025b reports reduced accuracy for every model evaluated, fine-tuned or zero-shot, in WIfI subcategories with κ below 0.4, consistent with label noise limiting performance. On the evaluation side, Basiri et al., 2025a reports Cohen's κ of 0.05–0.15 ("slight agreement") between two clinicians scoring model-generated descriptions of five DFU images, which is disagreement in outcome assessment and not in dataset labels.
mitigation_note: no consensus-labelling or noise-robust training method is tested

failure_mode: Automated metrics and LLM-judged quality disagree on which system is best
evidence: Durgapraveen et al., 2025 found an automated metric (deltaBLEU) and LLM-as-judge clinical-quality scoring disagreeing on which of two compared systems performed better. The authors recommend multi-faceted evaluation and lean toward the clinical-quality judgment ("clinical accuracy often supersedes surface-level text matching"), but propose no combined metric.
mitigation_note: the disagreement is interpreted informally, with no formal metric recommendation

failure_mode: A benchmark's own reported dataset size is internally inconsistent
evidence: Xu et al., 2026 states 697 images in its abstract, 686 in its Methods and Table 1, and a train/test/validation split of 480/173/69 that sums to 722; a separately stated 7:1:2 ratio reconciles with none of the three. Anyone citing this benchmark's exact scale should note the discrepancy.
mitigation_note: not identified or corrected by the source

failure_mode: Performance collapse on a naturalistic, predominantly Black-patient cohort
evidence: On a naturalistic dataset collected at a safety-net DFU clinic, predominantly from Black patients, Baseman et al., 2025's retrained Mask R-CNN baseline reached 39.5% Dice, against 90.2% reported for that architecture on the AZH Wound Care dataset in prior work; four further baselines fell from 72.9–90.3% to 18.3–36.0%. The authors' own adapted pipeline improved on every baseline and still reached only 54.4% Dice. The paper attributes the gap to naturalistic capture conditions, skin tone, and the small pixel share its wounds occupy, acting together. It is the corpus's only FM-track Validation paper built on a purpose-collected, demographically targeted dataset with an adapted pipeline.
mitigation_note: in the fairness sense: the paper re-trains extensively, which is its proposed contribution, but performs no skin-tone-stratified analysis and tests no tone-specific mitigation, listing subgroup fairness analysis as future work

failure_mode: External and cross-dataset validation is rare across the corpus, and not only for fairness
evidence: Only 4 of Validation's 18 tagged papers run any cross-dataset or external evaluation. Rates are similar at most steps checked: 0 of 5 in Acquisition, 2 of 57 in Model Selection, 3 of 22 in Adaptation Strategy, 2 of 19 in Output Formulation, and 1 of 8 in Deployment, where the one is a live real-world test. Preprocessing/QC is the exception at 2 of 4, a rate this survey attributes to that step's small sample size. Most papers validate models on data resembling their own training distribution, and the collapse in Entry 20 is one instance of that pattern.
mitigation_note: a field-level reporting gap with no norm, guideline, or incentive change proposed in the corpus

failure_mode: Race-based subgroup validation is not skin-tone validation, and the two are conflated
evidence: Muaddi et al., 2025's authors acknowledge that their bias analysis used patient-reported race in place of a Fitzpatrick or other skin-tone scale; in the paper's published discussant exchange the presenting author agrees that "race does not equal skin color at all" and states that Fitzpatrick stratification is in progress. Baseman et al., 2025 does not measure skin tone on a validated scale and describes its cohort's race only qualitatively ("predominantly collected from Black patients"), alongside a clinic-level figure of 80% non-Hispanic Black patients, with no per-patient breakdown.
mitigation_note: Muaddi et al., 2025's authors state that skin-tone stratification is underway; it has not been published

failure_mode: Discrimination metrics alone do not establish clinical rule-in/rule-out validity
evidence: Muaddi et al., 2025 reached an SSI-detection AUC of 0.81 while its recall was only 0.53, missing roughly half of actual surgical-site infections despite the favourable AUC. In the paper's published discussant exchange, one discussant asks whether the design target should be accuracy at all or ruling out infection, and the authors concede the model needs further refinement.
mitigation_note: debated in the discussant exchange, not resolved with a revised threshold or operating point

failure_mode: Accuracy and inter-run reliability are independent, non-substitutable dimensions for general-purpose MLLMs
evidence: Güler et al., 2026a's repeated-inference design (5 runs × 4 models × 50 burn images) found the two dissociated on burn depth: the most reliable model reached Fleiss' κ=0.916 without the highest accuracy, while the most accurate model was not the most reliable. The dissociation is task-specific and does not recur on the paper's total-body-surface-area task, so neither dimension should be read as a stable model property. Repeated inference is used only by this author team (both Güler et al. studies); single-query evaluation, used elsewhere in the corpus, cannot detect the dissociation.
mitigation_note: the repeated-inference design detects the dissociation without resolving which property to prioritize for deployment

failure_mode: Visual recognition capability does not transfer to clinical decision-making, even within one model on one image
evidence: Güler et al., 2026b found burn-depth classification exceeding a majority-class baseline in every one of four tested MLLMs (50.0–62.7% against 41.7%), while surgical-indication and treatment-recommendation accuracy fell below their baselines in every model. Surgical errors were overwhelmingly false negatives (52.6–75.8% sensitivity) in a cohort where 95% of cases required surgery, with negative predictive value never exceeding 14.8%. Full end-to-end pathway correctness reached 2.7–29.3%, so the perception-to-decision gap compounds along the clinical pathway.
mitigation_note: the gap is decomposed stage-by-stage; no intervention is tested

failure_mode: Tension between FM compute footprint and the field's stated low-compute deployment preference
evidence: Model Selection's FM evidence trends toward larger, heavier checkpoints, while the design target stated across Bansal and Vidyarthi, 2026, Borst et al., 2025 (WoundAIssist), and Borst et al., 2024 is small, fast, patient-facing, and edge-runnable. The step's one FM-track entry, Barua et al., 2026, restates the tension as a design goal ("optimized for edge execution") without naming or benchmarking a model that would satisfy it.

failure_mode: Offline benchmark metrics and real-world deployment behaviour rank models differently
evidence: Borst et al., 2024 compared seven model variants and found the lightweight architectures close together on held-out IoU and DSC, with U-Net leading, then judged the TopFormer family visually superior at distinguishing real wounds from wound-coloured decoy objects in a live six-scene phone test that no held-out metric captured. Downstream in the same group's pipeline, Borst et al., 2026 (WoundAmbit) selected VWFormer with a ConvNeXt-S backbone for production despite its placing fifth of twelve on out-of-distribution mIoU (77.2 against TransNeXt-Tiny's 79.4), because clinicians chose its masks as best most often (expert choice rate 35.0%, against 15.0% for the next model and 8.3% for TransNeXt).
mitigation_note: the group's workaround is to weight live-scene testing and clinician preference over offline benchmark rank; the live test covered six scenes, and the expert-choice comparison one reader study

failure_mode: Digital-divide and over-reliance risk, named by the authors themselves
evidence: Borst et al., 2025 (WoundAIssist) identify over-reliance on the app, including patients forgoing necessary in-person consultation and clinicians becoming less vigilant in verifying AI output, and unequal digital-device access and literacy, as risks of patient-facing AI-assisted wound care, distinct from and additional to the system's technical accuracy. These are raised in the paper's practical and societal impact discussion and were not measured in its usability studies.

failure_mode: Acquisition-stage class imbalance propagates directly into downstream segmentation quality
evidence: Chairat et al., 2023's calibration-and-correction pipeline improved cross-condition comparability overall, but downstream segmentation was tissue-type dependent: necrotic-tissue IoU (0.155) lagged far behind granulation-tissue IoU (0.642), which the authors attribute to the small amount of necrotic tissue in their own collected dataset and not to a calibration failure. Class weights assigned to the training loss did not close the gap.
mitigation_note: class-weighted training was attempted; no collection-side fix is tested

failure_mode: Automatic-capture uptake is platform-dependent, surfaced in a live clinical pilot
evidence: In Vasconcelos et al., 2024's real-time capture-guidance system, the share of images acquired in automatic mode was 85% on iOS against 44% on Android, with more failures at the focus stage on Android and mean acquisition time more than twice as long. This device-dependent gap surfaced in a prospective, real-device clinical pilot and was not visible in held-out benchmark evaluation.

failure_mode: A vision-capable model can decline to answer at a rate that accuracy computed over answered cases conceals
evidence: Apichonbancha et al., 2026 scored three frontier multimodal models on 450 wound photographs and recorded Gemini Advanced returning no usable output for 67–70% of images in most assessment domains and 88.2% on BWAT-framework scoring. A model answering one image in three is not comparable to one answering all of them, yet the two produce accuracy figures on the same scale. Few papers in this corpus report non-response alongside accuracy; Apichonbancha et al., 2026 and Takahashi et al., 2026, which reports parsed predictions for all 1,091 images under every model and prompt condition, are the exceptions.
mitigation_note: no reporting convention or metric adjustment is proposed
